summary: The measurement and the causal claim hold. Traced in code: BulkService.appendBulkBody appends per 1000-record chunk via a blocking Ingest.append (DefaultIngest.append parks on mine.done().join() until flushLocked completes), the accumulator is drained on that same flush, and firstAppendMillis resets to -1, so a lone producer genuinely advances exactly one chunk per interval and never holds more than one chunk. The arithmetic is internally consistent: 2,097,174 B at ~228 B/record is ~9,190 records = 9 full chunks + 1 partial = 10 appends = 10 flushes = 40 LocalFsBinStore files (data + .v per object, 2 objects per flush); 2,097,174/51.5 = 40.7 KB/s; 209,715,200/40,721 = 5,150 s = 86 min; 806 KiB/s (200 MiB / 254 s, M1.18's recorded figure) / 39.8 KiB/s = 20.3x. fillRatio 209,717/8,388,608 = 0.025 is in the low band, and adaptInterval's low branch re-assigns intervalCeiling on every subsequent drain, so the ceiling is indeed self-sustaining for a lone producer. ADR-0026 is a legitimate ADR: five rejected alternatives, each quantified, and its cost claim is correct -- nothing here changes the request pattern, which stays one PUT plus one commit delta per flush and scales with segments, not records/shards/partitions/indices. Two major findings, both about the REMEDY rather than the diagnosis: the prescribed load shape (arrivals exceeding 8 MiB per ceiling interval) forces fillRatio >= 1.0, which by this milestone's own criteria 1/3 and by Accumulator.adaptInterval with intervalShortenDelay = ZERO drops the interval to the 250 ms floor on that very flush -- so the state AC5 now names survives exactly one flush, and the one ceiling regime that IS sustainable (the middle band, which is the timer-bound case AC5 originally cared about) is the one the amendment excludes; and the ADR's stated justification for accepting the lone-producer slowdown -- 'only on a pod that has no meaningful traffic' -- is contradicted by criterion 4 in the same SPEC, where 1 MiB/s per pod settles at the ceiling as the designed steady state. Two minors recorded.

findings.title: The amended shape -- ceiling interval AND arrivals exceeding 8 MiB per interval -- is a state the M3.3 control loop dismantles on the first flush, and it excludes the only sustainable ceiling regime
findings.failure_scenario: AC5, the T12 row and the ADR's Decision all specify 'the interval warmed to its 5 s ceiling and enough concurrent producers that one interval's arrivals exceed the 8 MiB target, so the size trigger is what bounds the accumulator'. Trace it: Accumulator.isFlushDue fires on bufferedBytes >= maxSegmentBytes (8 MiB), drain() computes lastFillRatio = segment.length / 8 MiB >= 1.0, and adaptInterval takes the FIRST branch (lastFillRatio >= fillRatioHighThreshold 0.9); with IngestConfig.DEFAULT_INTERVAL_SHORTEN_DELAY = Duration.ZERO, nowMillis - highStreakStartMillis == 0 >= 0, so currentInterval = intervalFloor on that very drain. From the second flush onward the run is at 250 ms with ~400 KB segments -- fillRatio ~0.05, low band -- i.e. exactly M1.18's floor regime, until the 2-minute lengthen delay flips it back to the ceiling for one more size-triggered flush. So the prescribed regime holds for at most 1 flush in every ~480, and the SPEC's own claim that this is the regime where 'the size trigger rather than the timer' does the bounding, and the ADR's claim that it is 'the only one where the asserted bound is the bound actually doing the work', are both false. This is the same defect the amendment exists to remove, relocated: an implementer of M3.5 who follows the wording writes a long-running test believing it is at the ceiling while nearly all of it runs at the floor. Worse, the amendment discards the regime that DOES sustain the ceiling and IS what criterion 5 originally worried about: aggregate arrivals between ~0.64 and ~1.44 MiB/s put fillRatio strictly between 0.4 and 0.9, which hits adaptInterval's else branch (both streaks reset, currentInterval untouched), so the interval stays at 5 s indefinitely while the TIMER flushes a 3.2-7.2 MiB accumulator -- 'segments held open for up to 5 s, accumulating more before a flush than the fixed-250ms path ever did', verbatim the original criterion, now reachable AND sustainable with concurrent producers. That is also the SPEC's own worked load (criterion 4's 1 MiB/s per pod, ~5 MiB per ceiling flush, fillRatio ~0.6). Fix by specifying the arrival rate to land in the middle band rather than above the size trigger, or -- if the 8 MiB size-triggered peak is genuinely the intended measurement -- by saying in both files that the ceiling survives only that first flush and why the peak is still the right thing to sample.

findings.title: The ADR's justification for accepting the 40 KB/s lone-producer case is factually wrong and contradicts criterion 4 of the SPEC amended in the same commit
findings.failure_scenario: The Decision section accepts the property as-is on the grounds that 'the ceiling is reached only after two minutes of sustained low fillRatio, which is to say only on a pod that has no meaningful traffic, and one producer arriving at such a pod is by definition not the load this system is sized for.' The threshold says otherwise: fillRatio <= 0.4 means a drained segment under 3.355 MB, and at the 250 ms floor that is any pod ingesting less than ~13.4 MB/s. Every pod below that -- which is essentially the whole design envelope -- lengthens to the ceiling after 2 minutes. M3 SPEC criterion 4 states this explicitly for the project's own worked load ('at a modeled low-traffic load (1 MiB/s per pod, matching ADR-0017's own worked example), once the interval has settled at its 5 s ceiling'), and ADR-0017's $15.55/month headline IS the pod-at-the-ceiling steady state. So the ceiling is the NORMAL operating point at design load, not an idle-pod curiosity, and the ~45 KB/s per-connection cap (1000 records per 5 s flush) applies to every producer connection on a busy pod too, not just to a lone one on an empty pod -- a producer needs ~23 concurrent connections to push the 1 MiB/s per pod ADR-0017 sizes for. Consequence: a reader of this ADR (and the support engineer it was explicitly written for) concludes the slowdown cannot occur under real traffic and does not size producer concurrency, and the accept-as-is decision rests on a premise that the same commit's SPEC contradicts. The measurement and the 'record the property' half stand; the reason given for not fixing it needs replacing with the true one (this is a per-connection property, and throughput comes from connection concurrency).

findings.title: '~210 KB per chunk' is the run average including the short trailing chunk, not the chunk size; the ADR's own formula does not reproduce its own number
findings.failure_scenario: With M1.18's record shape (action line '{"index":{"_id":"d<i>","_version":1}}\n' = 35 + digits = 39 B at 4-digit ids, doc line '{"p":"' + 180 pad + '"}\n' = 189 B) a record is ~228 B, so a full APPEND_CHUNK_RECORDS chunk is ~228 KB, not ~210 KB. 209,717 B is the 10-flush average of a 2 MiB body whose last chunk carries only ~190 records. The ADR then states the property as 'APPEND_CHUNK_RECORDS x recordBytes / currentInterval', which evaluates to 1000 x 228 / 5.15 s = ~44 KB/s rather than the ~40 KB/s beside it, and the steady-state 200 MiB extrapolation is ~79 min rather than ~86 min. Nothing downstream changes -- both are 20x the floor and both are far past any usable gate -- but the ~210 KB figure is repeated four times across the ADR and the SPEC and is the number a future reader will reuse as 'the chunk size', which it is not.

findings.title: The Research: anchor does not resolve -- R1b is not in the file it points at
findings.failure_scenario: 'Research: docs/research/00-problem/02-cost-model.md#r1b'. That file contains no occurrence of the string R1b and no heading generating an #r1b anchor (its headings are '## 1. Unit prices' through '## 7. The cost meter'); R1b is defined in docs/internal/standards/cost.md line 11 ('R1b is the adaptive-interval rule'). check-links passed because it resolves the path, not the fragment. A reader following the pointer to check the arithmetic behind the interval-as-cost-dial lands in a document that never names the rule cited. The M3 SPEC's own cost section cites the same research file without a fragment, which is the citation that actually resolves.
